blocks.title: How a light microscope works
blocks.md: A **light microscope** shines light **through a thin specimen** on the **stage**. The **objective lens** forms an enlarged image which the **eyepiece lens** enlarges again. A **mirror or lamp** supplies light; the **coarse** and **fine focusing knobs** move the lens to make the image sharp. **Total magnification = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification**, e.g. ×10 × ×40 = ×400.

blocks.caption: A light microscope.
blocks.alt: A microscope with eyepiece lens, body tube, objective lens, arm, stage and mirror or lamp labelled.

blocks.title: Sizes and units
blocks.md: **Magnification = image size ÷ actual size**, so **actual size = image size ÷ magnification**. Use one unit: **1 mm = 1000 µm** (micrometres). Most animal and plant cells are 10 to 100 µm across; the smallest thing seen with a light microscope is about 0.2 µm. Example: a drawing 45 mm wide at ×150 is 45 ÷ 150 = **0.30 mm = 300 µm** in real life.

blocks.title: Using the microscope and drawing
blocks.md: Start with the **lowest-power objective**, lower it close to the slide while looking from the side, then focus **upwards**. Change to a higher power and use only the **fine focus**. **Drawing rules**: use a sharp pencil; draw large, clear single lines, no shading; draw only what you see; label with **ruled lines that do not cross**; give a **title** and the magnification.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Focusing **downwards** while looking through the eyepiece can break the slide.
- Do not add the magnifications: **multiply** them.
- Do not forget to convert mm to µm: 0.3 mm is 300 µm, not 3 µm.

lessons.title: Cell structure and organisation

objectives: Name the parts of animal and plant cells and state their functions.
Explain how specialised cells are adapted to their jobs.
Describe the levels of organisation in living things.
reviewNotes: Some syllabuses introduce organelles (ribosomes, endoplasmic reticulum) only later; check the level. Bacterial cell mention is minimal.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Parts of a cell
blocks.md:
- **Cell membrane**: controls what enters and leaves.
- **Cytoplasm**: where most chemical reactions happen.
- **Nucleus**: contains the **DNA** (genes) and controls the cell.
- **Mitochondria**: release energy in **respiration**.

**Plant cells** also have a **cell wall** of **cellulose** (support), **chloroplasts** with chlorophyll (photosynthesis) and a large **permanent vacuole** with cell sap. Animal cells have none of these three, but small temporary vacuoles. **Bacterial cells** have a cell wall but **no nucleus**.

blocks.caption: Six specialised cells and their jobs.
blocks.alt: Six boxes: red blood cell carries oxygen; white blood cell fights germs; nerve cell carries impulses; root hair cell absorbs water; palisade cell does photosynthesis; sperm cell fertilises the egg.

blocks.title: Specialised cells: structure fits function
blocks.md: A **red blood cell** has no nucleus and is a flattened disc, giving more room for **haemoglobin** and a large surface area. A **root hair cell** has a long thin extension that increases the surface for absorbing water. A **palisade cell** is packed with chloroplasts near the top of the leaf. A **nerve cell** has a long fibre to carry messages. A **sperm cell** has a tail to swim and many mitochondria.

blocks.caption: Levels of organisation from cell to organism.
blocks.alt: Five boxes joined by arrows: cell (muscle cell), tissue (muscle), organ (heart), system (circulatory), organism (person).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The cell wall is **not** the cell membrane: all cells have a membrane, only plants and bacteria have a wall.
- A tissue is a group of **similar cells**; an organ has **several tissues**.
- Mature red blood cells have no nucleus, but they are still cells.

blocks.title: Identify the cell
blocks.statement: A cell has a nucleus, a cell wall, many chloroplasts and a large vacuole. Is it an animal or a plant cell? Which job does it probably do?
steps: The cell wall, chloroplasts and large vacuole are plant features.
Many chloroplasts show it makes food by photosynthesis, like a palisade cell.
blocks.answer: A plant cell, probably a palisade cell, making food.

blocks.title: Adaptation
blocks.statement: Explain how a red blood cell is adapted to carry oxygen.
steps: It contains haemoglobin which combines with oxygen.
It has no nucleus and is disc-shaped, giving more space for haemoglobin and a large surface area.
blocks.answer: Haemoglobin, no nucleus, large surface area.
